recipe: Every program's purpose is transforming data. If you don't understand the data, you don't understand the problem. Understand the data first, the transformation second, the code last.

recipe: Three lies: software is a platform, code should model the world, code matters more than data. Hardware is the platform. Data is the problem. Code is only the transformation.

recipe: Where there is one, there are many. Design the array first, the single item second. Look along the time axis too: one thing across many frames is also many.

question: Are there multiple instances of the same item?

recipe: Solve for the actual data in the common case, not the general case. Generic solutions to imagined future data cost real performance now. Future-proofing is speculation, not engineering.
raw: Does the code process data outside the common case?
question: Does the code process data outside the common case?

recipe: If you don't understand the cost of the data, you don't understand the cost of the problem. A main-memory miss costs hundreds of cycles; arithmetic is nearly free beside it.
raw: Does the code access large data from main memory?
question: Does the code access large data from main memory?

recipe: The compiler is not magic. It fixes roughly a tenth of your performance problem and cannot fix memory layout. It doesn't know your data; you do.
raw: Does the performance problem involve memory layout?
question: Does the performance problem involve memory layout?

recipe: Prefer structure-of-arrays. Split a record by access pattern so a pass over one field touches only cache lines it will actually use. Array-of-structures drags cold bytes through cache.
raw: Does the hot loop access only one field per record?
question: Does the hot loop access only one field per record?

recipe: Hot/cold split: fields touched every tick live in one array; rarely-read fields live elsewhere, reached by index. Cold data inside a hot loop is pure wasted bandwidth.
raw: Does the hot loop read rarely-read fields?
question: Does the hot loop read rarely-read fields?

recipe: Avoid pointer chasing. Replace pointers with indices into arrays: smaller, relocatable, serializable, prefetchable. A linked structure is one cache miss per node with no prefetch.
raw: Does the code traverse linked nodes by following pointers?
question: Does the code traverse linked nodes by following pointers?

recipe: Shrink your handles. u32 or even u16 indices are usually enough and cost a quarter to half of a 64-bit pointer. Smaller elements mean more of them per cache line.
Order struct fields by descending alignment to kill padding. Count the wasted bytes explicitly. A struct that drops under a cache line changes the behaviour of the entire loop.
Zig's MultiArrayList is the pattern worth stealing: one logical list, one array per field, same API, padding gone. Reach for that before hand-splitting a struct.
Transform in bulk. One function over N items beats N virtual calls over one item: amortized branches, warm instruction cache, obvious vectorization, prefetch that actually works.
Existence-based processing: don't store a flag and branch on it. Store the entity in the table for that state. Presence is the predicate, so the loop has no if.
raw: Does the code branch on a boolean flag?
question: Does the code branch on a boolean flag?

recipe: Branching is a memory-layout problem. Sort or partition so each pass is homogeneous; the branch then disappears instead of being mispredicted a million times per frame.
raw: Does the loop branch on a per-item field?

recipe: Condition tables over nested ifs: express decisions as rows of conditions and consequences, then evaluate them as data. Branch-light, inspectable, hot-reloadable, extendable without touching code.

recipe: Your data is already a database; you just hid it inside objects. Normalize: entities get ids, relationships get tables. Schema-first exposes multiplicity and frees layout from the class.

recipe: Any data structure is a trade between performance, readability, maintenance, extensibility and reuse. Name which one you are buying before you defend the layout you picked.

recipe: The primary t comes first: Map.find t key, Queue.enqueue t x. Uniform argument order beats locally optimal partial application; predictability is worth more than one clever pipeline.

The unsuffixed name is total and returns an option; _exn marks the raising twin. Map.find versus Map.find_exn. The suffix is the warning, visible at the call site.
Use _opt when the plain name is already taken by the raising one: of_string raises, of_string_opt returns None. Never a sentinel, never -1, never null.

recipe: Before profiling: release build, lto = "thin" or "fat", codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort". -C target-cpu=native buys AVX at the cost of portability. PGO adds roughly ten percent.
C-GENERIC: take generics, not concrete types; AsRef<str> over &String. C-CALLER-CONTROL: the caller decides where data is copied and placed. Collections implement FromIterator and Extend.
C-ITER: collections expose iter / iter_mut / into_iter. C-ITER-TY: name the iterator type after the method producing it. Conversions go through From, AsRef, AsMut.
Split hot fields from cold ones so the cache line carries only what the loop reads. Drepper measures up to 5x. Run pahole and close the holes.
Put the most likely critical member first in the struct, and read members in declaration order, so the critical word arrives first out of the cache line.

question: Does the code read a struct's critical member first?

recipe: Align big arrays to the cache line: posix_memalign, or __attribute__((aligned(64))) for automatics. Unaligned access costs 20-30% on large working sets, far worse streaming out of L2.

recipe: Do not hardcode 64. Query sysconf(_SC_LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE) at runtime, or getconf at build time, then derive your blocking factor from it.

question: Does the loop touch all fields of each item?

recipe: Keep hot variables local so they live on the stack and likely in L1. Avoid globals, statics, and dynamic allocation for data that is used together.

question: Are hot variables allocated outside the local stack?

recipe: malloc/free in hot code costs far more than stack storage, fragments the heap, and wrecks caching. Hoist the allocation out of the loop and reuse the buffer.
raw: Does the hot loop allocate memory?
question: Does the hot loop allocate memory?

recipe: Many small variable-size objects, strings especially: put them all in one memory pool. A malloc per object is where the fragmentation and heap-management overhead comes from.

question: Are many small variable-size objects allocated separately?

recipe: Short-lived variable-size array: alloca puts it on the stack. No fragmentation, free deallocation, contiguous with other stack data. Never return a pointer into it; check your compiler's restrictions.

question: Is the variable-size array short-lived?

recipe: Access sequentially. Backwards is slower, random much slower. Multidimensional arrays: last index in the innermost loop. Do not swap those two loops.

question: Does the code access a multidimensional array?

recipe: A matrix row stride that is a high power of two hits the critical stride and thrashes cache sets; transposes and tiled kernels stall. Pad the row or block the loop.
raw: Is the matrix row stride a high power of two?
question: Is the matrix row stride a high power of two?

recipe: Misprediction costs roughly 15-25 cycles; a predicted branch costs 0-2. Compute the condition early, prefer integer comparisons over float, and keep 50/50 branches out of the hot loop.

question: Does the hot loop contain a branch with a 50/50 outcome?

recipe: Reach for __builtin_expect only where profiling is impossible. GCC's own manual says programmers are notoriously bad at predicting this; prefer -fprofile-arcs feedback.

question: Is profiling impossible here?

recipe: Auto-vectorization needs: restrict pointers, no element-level branches or table lookups, trip count divisible by the vector width, arrays aligned 32 for AVX and 64 for AVX512. Read the asm.
restrict on non-overlapping pointer parameters lets the compiler drop the reload after every store and vectorize. It is a promise, not a hint: alias through it and behavior is undefined.

recipe: Predictable but non-sequential reads: _mm_prefetch(ptr, _MM_HINT_T0). Write-once data you will not re-read: non-temporal stores such as _mm_stream_si128, to avoid polluting the cache.

question: Does the code read predictable but non-sequential data?

recipe: Hardware prefetchers cannot cross page boundaries and need a recognizable pattern. Tile loops by cache line: SM = CLS/sizeof(elem). Drepper's tiled matmul hit roughly ten percent of original time.

recipe: Per.16, Per.18, Per.19: compact data structures, space is time, access memory predictably. Row-major traversal with the inner loop over columns; the transposed version is the classic cache-miss bug.

recipe: F.18: will-move-from parameters take X&& and std::move inside. ES.56: write std::move only to move across scopes. F.48: never return std::move(local), it blocks copy elision.
F.16: cheap-to-copy in-parameters by value, everything else by const reference. F.20: return values, not out-parameters. F.21: return a struct for multiple outputs.
Per.11 and F.4: move computation from run time to compile time. constexpr initialization removes both the runtime call and the static-init data race. You cannot race on a constant.
Per.7, design to enable optimization: qsort throws away the element type and forces an indirect call per compare; a template sort keeps the type and inlines the comparison.

SAB-backed TypedArray stores cross workers with no copy; query(world,[A,B],asBuffer) returns Uint32Array ready to postMessage. Partition one query's entities per worker and never let a thread write data another reads. addEntity/addComponent are main-thread only.
